summary: This RFC introduces the Host-Front End Protocol, described in detail in RFC 929. It was designed by a committee of experienced designers for the DoD, with the intent that it be tested through multiple implementations and revised.

plainLanguage.summary: A big computer can hand its network chores to a helper machine in front of it. This note introduces the rules for how they talk.

questions: what is the host front end protocol
subtitle: How to talk to an outboard processor that runs your network protocols for you.

tldr.problem: Big computers waste valuable cycles running network protocols, and different host types need different implementations. It would be better to offload all that protocol work to a dedicated helper machine, but how do you standardize the conversation between the host and the helper?
tldr.mechanism: The Host-Front End Protocol (H-FP) defines three layers: a physical Link layer for moving bits, a Channel layer for multiplexing connections, and a Command layer where the host and its outboard processor exchange ASCII commands and responses to manage connections and data flow.
tldr.outcome: H-FP allows different hosts to reuse the same network processor hardware and software, saves CPU time on resource-constrained systems, and insulates hosts from changes to underlying protocols. RFC 929 specifies the actual protocol; this RFC introduces the ideas.

today: RFC 928 is Historic. While the outboard processor approach did not become the dominant model for network protocol implementation (inboard TCP/IP stacks became standard), the concepts of protocol separation and the command-layer abstraction had lasting influence on later network architecture discussions.

sections.title: Outboard Processing Concept
sections.content:
RFC 928 introduces the Host-Front End Protocol (H-FP), a proposal for standardizing how a host computer talks to an outboard processor (also called a Network Front End or Outboard Processing Environment). Rather than embedding TCP, FTP, and other network protocol code inside the host's operating system—where it consumes CPU cycles and memory—the idea is to run all that code on a separate, specialized processor sitting between the host and the network.

The protocol was designed by a committee of experienced implementers at the DoD Protocol Standards Technical Panel. This is an introductory RFC; RFC 929 contains the detailed protocol specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of teaching every computer how to talk on the network, let one specialist machine handle all the networking, and every computer just talks to that specialist.

sections.title: Origins of Network Front Ends
sections.content:
The idea of separating network protocol processing from the host computer originated in 1971 during discussions about implementing the Network Control Program (NCP) on Multics. As computers became more capable, the opportunity arose to implement protocol handling on dedicated processors with plenty of space, avoiding disputes over specification interpretation and saving the host's CPU resources.

By the time this RFC was written, at least half a dozen different Host-Front End protocols had been fielded. The 1982 meeting that led to this RFC brought together the developers of those H-FPs to extract common principles and create a DoD standard. While outboard processing is not the only way to do networking, it offers clear advantages when CPU or memory is constrained, or when the same protocol code should run on many different host types.
sections.plainLanguage: In the 1970s, people noticed that if you put all the network code on one separate machine, you could reuse it for many different kinds of computers, and nobody had to argue about how it should work.

sections.title: Three-Layer Model
sections.content:
H-FP defines three separable layers. The bottom Link layer provides the physical means to send bits between host and processor—typically a bit-serial interface, but parallel or DMA links are possible. The middle Channel layer multiplexes network connections and manages flow control between host and processor, ensuring reliable delivery. This layer can optionally use the X.25 protocol if the host already supports it.

The top Command layer is the core of H-FP: it carries ASCII strings (not binary headers) that allow the host to issue commands and the processor to return responses. The host uses this layer to open connections, close them, send data, and manage the outboard protocol implementation. This text-based approach makes it easier for hosts with limited resources to implement the interface—even a simple script can control the processor.
sections.plainLanguage: The three layers are like levels of a company: Link is the mail room that moves physical envelopes, Channel is the routing department that delivers envelopes to the right office, and Command is the manager's office where decisions get made and reported back.

sections.title: ASCII Commands, Not Binary Headers
sections.content:
Unlike earlier H-FPs that used binary-encoded message headers, the new H-FP protocol uses ASCII strings as commands. This design choice came from experience with network protocols that already use text (like FTP) and from the observation that text commands are easier to parse, parse variable-length parameters naturally, and even allow straightforward terminal-based or script-driven interfaces.

Commands are simple ASCII strings, and responses are ASCII-encoded numbers (following the FTP model). This means a host need not be a full program; it could be a shell script or command file on systems that lack sophisticated networking applications. It reflects the original principle of H-FP design: making things as easy as possible for the host.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of sending confusing binary codes that only a computer can read, the helper machine understands simple English-like commands, so even a simple host can talk to it with just a script.

sections.title: Benefits of Outboarding
sections.content:
Outboard processing offers several advantages. Code reuse is paramount: a single, well-tested implementation of TCP/IP can serve many different host types, reducing procurement problems in the DoD context. Resource conservation is critical for hosts with limited CPU or memory; the protocol work happens on the specialized processor. Insulation from change protects the host: if TCP is replaced by a different transport protocol (say, ECMA Class 4), the host and its H-FP interface need not change.

For security architectures that require controlling all network ingress and egress, uniform use of outboard processors is desirable. The processor can enforce security policy consistently across many hosts. And for interoperability across different protocol families (DoD TCP/IP versus emerging ISO protocols), a multiprotocol processor can bridge the gap without burdening each host.
sections.plainLanguage: If one machine knows how to talk to the network, you can save the big computer's strength for what it's good at, you can swap out networking tricks without rewriting every computer, and you can enforce security rules in one place.

sections.title: Remaining Questions
sections.content:
Several design choices remain open for discussion and testing. The text-based command encoding was inspired by successful deployment but is uncommon enough that some reviewers find it unfamiliar. The use of X.25 for the Channel layer is appealing for hosts that already have X.25 software, but vendor X.25 implementations are not uniform, and bit-transfer rates are uncertain.

The RFC identifies issues around command syntax (which should be scrutinized in review), whether to modify the existing DCA/DTI Channel layer header, how much L III (application layer) offloading H-FP should support, handling of security labels in multilevel-secure environments, and the critical challenge of ensuring that H-FP actually implements more efficiently on the host side than the protocols being offloaded.

The RFC emphasizes that this is a proposal, not a standard: true consensus requires multiple independent test implementations and iteration based on real-world experience.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors admit some parts might need tweaking once people try to build it, and they definitely want feedback on whether it's simpler than the old way.
